fetched_contents.text: Using Conjunctions | Definition, Rules & Examples Published on October 23, 2022 by Amy Luo. Revised on March 8, 2023. A conjunction is a word that is used to connect words, phrases, and clauses. There are many conjunctions in the English language, but some common ones include and, or, but, because, for, if, and when. There are three basic types of conjunctions: coordinating, subordinating, and correlative. Because the popstar caught a terrible cold, her upcoming performances in Boston and Chicago were indefinitely postponed. The tour organizers provided neither rescheduled dates nor refunds for the tickets, causing much discontent among the fans. Coordinating conjunctions This type of conjunction is used to connect items that are grammatically equal: two words, two phrases, or two independent clauses. There are seven coordinating conjunctions in English, and you can remember them using the mnemonic device FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. A conjunction of this type is placed between the items that it links together. Words Coordinating conjunctions can join two nouns, verbs, adjectives, or other types of word. * The data was gathered through questionnaires and interviews. * I don’t like to run or swim. * He was clever but lazy. Phrases They can also join different types of phrases. * The dog wagged his tail and panted excitedly. * The results were undeniably intriguing yet ultimately inconclusive. * She usually studies in the library or at a cafe. Independent clauses A clause is a group of words that contains at least a subject and a verb. An independent clause can stand on its own as a full sentence, expressing a complete thought. * Today Jane Austen is one of the most widely read English novelists, but she achieved little fame during her lifetime. In the sentence above, the coordinating conjunction but creates a relationship between two independent clauses. Therefore, you place a comma before but. Notice that the two clauses also work as sentences on their own. * Today Jane Austen is one of the most widely read English novelists. She achieved little fame during her lifetime. Punctuating coordinating conjunctions When joining two words or phrases with a coordinating conjunction, do not use a comma. * Comma error * Correction Data was gathered through questionnaires, and interviews. Data was gathered through questionnaires and interviews. She usually studies in the library, or at a cafe. She usually studies in the library or at a cafe. In these examples, the conjunction joins two words or phrases that are connected to a single verb (gathered and studies), so you shouldn’t place a comma before and. When joining two independent clauses, however, use a comma before the conjunction. * Comma error * Correction Data was gathered through questionnaires and selected Data was gathered through questionnaires, and selected respondents participated in interviews. respondents participated in interviews. She usually studies in the library but when it is too busy She usually studies in the library, but when it is too busy she goes to a cafe. she goes to a cafe. In these examples, the clauses before and after the conjunction could both stand as full sentences on their own, so a comma is required. Subordinating conjunctions This type of conjunction includes words like because, if, although, since, until, and while. A subordinating conjunction is used to introduce a dependent clause. In contrast to an independent clause, a dependent clause (also known as a subordinate clause) is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb but cannot stand as a complete sentence on its own. A dependent clause does not express a complete idea, so it must always be attached to an independent clause. * Because I woke up late this morning. I went to school without eating breakfast. * Because I woke up late this morning, I went to school without eating breakfast. * I went to school without eating breakfast because I woke up late this morning. I woke up late this morning is an independent clause, but the subordinating conjunction because turns it into a dependent clause: Because I woke up late this morning does not finish a complete thought. It must be joined to an independent clause to form a grammatically correct sentence. The subordinating conjunction defines the relationship between the clauses. The table below shows some common subordinating conjunctions and the relationships they express, but note that this is not a complete list. In general, when the dependent clause contains essential information about the independent clause, don’t use a comma. * Comma error * Correction She will receive a major bonus, if she succeeds in closing She will receive a major bonus if she succeeds in closing the corporate partnership deal. the corporate partnership deal. John’s friends snuck into his apartment to set up a surprise John’s friends snuck into his apartment to set up a surprise party, while he was at work. party while he was at work. fetched_contents.text: Temporal Logic (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy/Fall 2019 Edition) 1. Temporal reasoning from antiquity to modern days Discussion of temporality and reasoning about time goes back to antiquity and examples can be found even in the Bible (Boyd 2014). Some of Zeno’s paradoxical arguments refer to the nature of time and the question of infinite divisibility of time intervals. Perhaps the earliest scientific reference on temporal reasoning, however, is Aristotle’s argument in On Interpretation, Ch. 9, that future contingents, i.e., statements about possible future events which may or may not occur, such as “There will be a sea-fight tomorrow”, should not be ascribed definite truth values at the present time. A few decades later the philosopher Diodorus Cronus (ca 340–280 BC) from the Megarian school demonstrated the problem of future contingents in his famous Master Argument where, inter alia, he defined “possible” as “what is or will ever be” and “necessary” as “what is and will always be”. For details, see Rescher and Urquhart (1971, Chapter XVII) and the entry on future contingents. Philosophical discussion on temporality, truth, free will, determinism, and how they are related, continued during the Middle ages. William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) argued that propositions about the contingent future cannot be known by humans as true or false because only God knows their truth value now. However, he argued that humans still have some freedom of choice amongst different possible futures, thus suggesting the idea of a future-branching model of time with many possible time-lines (histories), truth of propositions being relativised to a possible actual history; this model of time is now often called Ockhamist. Later, several philosophers and logicians, including C. S. Peirce, raised and analysed problems relating temporality with non-determinism, historical necessity, free will, God’s will and knowledge, etc., proposing various different solutions. ## Branch on semantic interpretation of simultaneity and sequence

The semantic interpretation of temporal conjunctions such as “when,” “before,” and “after” is best understood as a combination of temporal relation and discourse structure. In the evidence, these conjunctions encode different kinds of temporal ordering: “before” and “after” are primarily used to express precedence and succession, while “when” is more ambiguous and can sometimes imply simultaneity or a time frame within which an event occurs [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The clearest semantic distinction is that “before” and “after” are explicitly about ordering two events in time, whereas “when” can also describe a point in time or a temporal frame in which something happens [N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Semantic relation: simultaneity, precedence, succession
The evidence shows that “when” is especially sensitive to ambiguity because it can encode either a moment of simultaneity or a temporal frame. The glossa article on temporal adverbial clauses notes that “when” before/after takes a clause and that its complement is quantificational and raises to a higher position, which implies that it is not simply a static time point but a clause-level temporal relation [N2-R1]. That reading supports the idea that “when” can anchor a subordinate clause to a broader time window rather than a single instant. In contrast, “before” and “after” are more clearly ordering markers: they establish that one event occurs earlier or later than another. The same source also states that “when before/after” inverts the order of events and raises to a higher position, reinforcing that these conjunctions are used to compare events across time [N2-R1]. The temporal adverbial clauses survey further distinguishes these conjunctions as part of the broader set of temporal relations, including “until,” “since,” and “as soon as,” and notes that they can also co-occur with non-temporal relations such as “if,” “although,” and “in order to,” but the temporal ones are still primarily about time order [N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Ambiguity and context
Ambiguity is a central theme. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that temporal expressions are often underspecified and that interpretation depends on context. For example, the study on inferred temporal order in complex sentences notes that people infer temporal order from sometimes underspecified linguistic information, which means that the same phrase can be read differently depending on what else is present in the discourse [N3-R3]. This directly supports the claim that context can change the interpretation of temporal expressions. The glossa article also notes that “when before/after” raises to a higher position, which implies that the relation is not fixed by the clause alone but is shaped by surrounding information [N2-R1]. The temporal adverbial clauses survey similarly states that “when” before/after clauses can be interpreted differently depending on whether the clause is seen as a temporal or non-temporal structure [N2-R4]. Taken together, the evidence shows that “when,” “before,” and “after” are semantically flexible, and their interpretation is often context-sensitive rather than fixed by syntax alone.

### Differences between “before,” “after,” and “when”
The main difference between “before” and “after” is that both express a clear temporal ordering: “before” means one event precedes another, while “after” means it follows. The evidence does not distinguish them as sharply in terms of scope, but it does show that they are both clause-level temporal markers rather than simple adverbs. In contrast, “when” is more open-ended because it can function as a point-in-time marker, a time frame marker, or a clause-level temporal relation [N2-R1][N2-R3]. The temporal adverbial clauses survey notes that “when” is one of the temporal relations in the set with “before,” “after,” “until,” “since,” and “as soon as,” but it is still distinct because it often interacts with clause structure in a way that makes its interpretation more ambiguous [N2-R3]. The glossa article also states that “when before/after” takes a clause and that its complement is quantificational, which suggests that “when” can sometimes operate on a more abstract or generalized temporal relation than “before” and “after” [N2-R1].

### Tense or aspect interaction
Tense and aspect do interact with the semantic reading, though the evidence here is indirect. The glossa article notes that temporal adverbial clauses raise to a higher position and that their complements can be quantificational, which implies that tense and temporal structure are not independent: the clause itself can impose a temporal reading on the surrounding sentence [N2-R1]. The temporal logic overview in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy further shows that temporal reasoning is deeply tied to logical structure, and that temporal adverbials modify or change the aspectual class of the core proposition [N4-R3]. The evidence also suggests that temporal adverbials can interact with aspect in a more fine-grained way, such that they can change the aspecmal class of the proposition rather than simply adding a time stamp [N4-R3]. However, the available evidence does not give a detailed account of how each conjunction interacts with tense or aspect in English, so the claim should be stated carefully: the semantic reading is shaped by tense and aspect, but the evidence here is strongest for the broader claim that temporal relations are not purely lexical or syntactic [N2-R1][N4-R3].

## Overall conclusion
The semantic branch suggests that “before” and “after” are primarily ordering markers expressing precedence and succession, while “when” is more flexible and can encode simultaneity, a time frame, or a clause-level temporal relation. Ambiguity and context are central to interpretation, and tense and aspect can interact with the semantic reading, though the evidence here is stronger for the general claim than for a detailed grammatical interaction. The strongest supported claim is that these conjunctions are semantically tied to clause structure and discourse context, not just simple adverbials [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4][N3-R3].

## Branch on syntactic behavior of temporal conjunctions

The syntactic behavior of “when,” “before,” and “after” is best characterized as subordinate-clause temporal markers, but they differ in how they introduce clauses and how they interact with tense and clause order. The evidence shows that all three are typically used to introduce subordinate clauses, and that their complements can be clause-level structures rather than isolated adverbs [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R4]. At the same time, the evidence also suggests that their syntactic behavior is shaped by clause structure, tense, and discourse organization.

### How each conjunction introduces or relates clauses
The syntactic evidence is consistent that “when,” “before,” and “after” are subordinating conjunctions used to introduce subordinate clauses. The Scribbr entry explicitly lists them as subordinating conjunctions in the “time” category, along with “once,” “until,” “whenever,” “since,” and “while” [N1-R2]. The same source also explains that a subordinating conjunction introduces a dependent clause and that the dependent clause cannot stand alone as a complete sentence [N1-R2]. The glossa article on temporal adverbial clauses states that “when before/after” takes a clause and that its complement is quantificational and raises to a higher position [N2-R1]. This supports the idea that “when,” “before,” and “after” are not merely prepositional or adverbial markers; they introduce clause-level temporal relations. The temporal adverbial clauses survey similarly notes that these conjunctions are part of the set of temporal relations used to express temporal adverbial clauses, including “until,” “since,” and “as soon as” [N2-R3][N2-R4]. Taken together, the evidence shows that all three conjunctions primarily function as clause-introducing temporal markers rather than simple adverbs.

### Whether they head a subordinate clause or function as a temporal adverbial
The evidence clearly supports the subordinate-clause interpretation. The Scribbr entry explains that subordinating conjunctions introduce dependent clauses and that dependent clauses cannot stand alone as complete sentences [N1-R2]. The glossa article further notes that “when before/after” takes a clause and that its complement is quantificational and raises to a higher position, which is consistent with a subordinate-clause structure [N2-R1]. The temporal adverbial clauses survey likewise lists them as temporal relations used in temporal adverbial clauses, reinforcing that they are clause-level rather than purely adverbial [N2-R3][N2-R4]. Thus, the best-supported conclusion is that these conjunctions head subordinate clauses or function as clause-introducing temporal adverbials, not as standalone adverbs.

### How syntax handles overlapping or nested temporal expressions

The glossa article states that “when before/after” takes a clause and that its complement is quantificational and raises to a higher position, implying that multiple temporal markers can co-occur and interact in a hierarchical or coordinated way [N2-R1]. This implies that nested or overlapping temporal expressions can be handled through clause ordering, topic/focus structure, and discourse organization rather than a single linear sequence [N5-F4]. The evidence is therefore consistent with the idea that overlapping temporal expressions are possible in syntax, but they are resolved through clause structure, clause order, and discourse organization rather than a simple concatenation of markers.

### Whether the clause is tensed or tenseless in the main clause
The evidence is less direct on tenseless structures, but it is clear that the main clause can be tensed in the usual English pattern. The Scribbr entry notes that the verb in the time clause is usually in the present tense, while the main clause can be in the future or past [N1-R3]. This is the standard English pattern for temporal adverbial clauses: the subordinate clause is often present tense, and the main clause is tensed accordingly [N1-R3]. The glossa article also discusses the interpretation of tense in temporal adverbial clauses, noting that the complement is quantificational and raises to a higher position, which suggests that tense is part of the clause structure rather than simply a lexical property [N2-R1]. The temporal adverbial clauses survey further notes that these conjunctions are used in temporal adverbial clauses, which implies that tense is a relevant component of the clause structure [N2-R3]. The evidence does not provide a detailed account of tenseless languages, so the safest conclusion is that in English, the main clause is tensed, and the subordinate clause is often present-tense, with tense playing a role in the overall temporal interpretation [N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R3].

## Overall conclusion
The syntactic branch shows that “when,” “before,” and “after” are primarily subordinate-clause temporal markers, not standalone adverbs. They introduce or relate clauses in a sentence, often raising the complement to a higher position or treating it as a quantificational clause [N2-R1][N2-R4]. They can handle overlapping or nested temporal expressions through clause structure and discourse organization [N4-R1][N5-F4]. In English, the main clause is typically tensed, while the subordinate clause is often present-tense, and tense is part of the overall clause structure [N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R3].

The evidence indicates that simultaneity and sequence are marked in ways that vary across languages. This cross-linguistic evidence supports the claim that simultaneity and sequence are not encoded in a single universal way, but are realized differently across languages.

### What theoretical frameworks explain these patterns
The evidence points to several theoretical frameworks. First, temporal logic provides a formal framework for representing temporal relations and reasoning about time [N4-R2][N4-R5]. Second, discourse marker studies show that temporal markers such as “after,” “before,” or “while” are often treated as triggers for discourse relations expressing temporal order [N5-R4]. Third, comparative linguistics and temporal reference studies show that languages differ in how they mark temporal reference, including whether they use tense, aspect, or clause structure [N5-R1]. ### How comparison illuminates universal versus language-specific behavior
The cross-linguistic comparison in the evidence helps distinguish universal tendencies from language-specific behavior. The cross-linguistic temporal reference review explicitly states that the review catalogues means affecting temporal reference across tensed and tenseless languages and offers a theoretical perspective on temporal reference [N5-R1]. The temporal logic overview further suggests that temporal constructions are complex and can be studied formally, which supports the view that certain temporal relations are likely universal, but their grammatical realization is not [N4-R1][N4-R5]. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that cross-linguistic comparison is useful for identifying both universal constraints and language-specific strategies for expressing simultaneity and sequence [N5-R1][N5-R4][N4-R1][N4-R5].

## Overall conclusion

The semantic interpretation of temporal conjunctions such as “when,” “before,” and “after” is best understood as a combination of temporal relation and discourse structure. In the evidence, these conjunctions encode different kinds of temporal ordering: “before” and “after” are primarily used to express precedence and succession, while “when” is more ambiguous and can sometimes imply simultaneity or a time frame within which an event occurs [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The clearest semantic distinction is that “before” and “after” are explicitly about ordering two events in time, whereas “when” can also describe a point in time or a temporal frame in which something happens [N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Semantic relation: simultaneity, precedence, succession
The evidence shows that “when” is especially sensitive to ambiguity because it can encode either a moment of simultaneity or a temporal frame. The glossa article on temporal adverbial clauses notes that “when” before/after takes a clause and that its complement is quantificational and raises to a higher position, which implies that it is not simply a static time point but a clause-level temporal relation [N2-R1]. That reading supports the idea that “when” can anchor a subordinate clause to a broader time window rather than a single instant. In contrast, “before” and “after” are more clearly ordering markers: they establish that one event occurs earlier or later than another. The same source also states that “when before/after” inverts the order of events and raises to a higher position, reinforcing that these conjunctions are used to compare events across time [N2-R1]. The temporal adverbial clauses survey further distinguishes these conjunctions as part of the broader set of temporal relations, including “until,” “since,” and “as soon as,” and notes that they can also co-occur with non-temporal relations such as “if,” “although,” and “in order to,” but the temporal ones are still primarily about time order [N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Ambiguity and context
Ambiguity is a central theme. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that temporal expressions are often underspecified and that interpretation depends on context. For example, the study on inferred temporal order in complex sentences notes that people infer temporal order from sometimes underspecified linguistic information, which means that the same phrase can be read differently depending on what else is present in the discourse [N3-R3]. This directly supports the claim that context can change the interpretation of temporal expressions. The glossa article also notes that “when before/after” raises to a higher position, which implies that the relation is not fixed by the clause alone but is shaped by surrounding information [N2-R1]. The temporal adverbial clauses survey similarly states that “when” before/after clauses can be interpreted differently depending on whether the clause is seen as a temporal or non-temporal structure [N2-R4]. Taken together, the evidence shows that “when,” “before,” and “after” are semantically flexible, and their interpretation is often context-sensitive rather than fixed by syntax alone.

### Differences between “before,” “after,” and “when”
The main difference between “before” and “after” is that both express a clear temporal ordering: “before” means one event precedes another, while “after” means it follows. The evidence does not distinguish them as sharply in terms of scope, but it does show that they are both clause-level temporal markers rather than simple adverbs. In contrast, “when” is more open-ended because it can function as a point-in-time marker, a time frame marker, or a clause-level temporal relation [N2-R1][N2-R3]. The temporal adverbial clauses survey notes that “when” is one of the temporal relations in the set with “before,” “after,” “until,” “since,” and “as soon as,” but it is still distinct because it often interacts with clause structure in a way that makes its interpretation more ambiguous [N2-R3]. The glossa article also states that “when before/after” takes a clause and that its complement is quantificational, which suggests that “when” can sometimes operate on a more abstract or generalized temporal relation than “before” and “after” [N2-R1].

### Tense or aspect interaction
Tense and aspect do interact with the semantic reading, though the evidence here is indirect. The glossa article notes that temporal adverbial clauses raise to a higher position and that their complements can be quantificational, which implies that tense and temporal structure are not independent: the clause itself can impose a temporal reading on the surrounding sentence [N2-R1]. The temporal logic overview in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy further shows that temporal reasoning is deeply tied to logical structure, and that temporal adverbials modify or change the aspectual class of the core proposition [N4-R3]. The evidence also suggests that temporal adverbials can interact with aspect in a more fine-grained way, such that they can change the aspecmal class of the proposition rather than simply adding a time stamp [N4-R3]. However, the available evidence does not give a detailed account of how each conjunction interacts with tense or aspect in English, so the claim should be stated carefully: the semantic reading is shaped by tense and aspect, but the evidence here is strongest for the broader claim that temporal relations are not purely lexical or syntactic [N2-R1][N4-R3].

## Overall conclusion
The semantic branch suggests that “before” and “after” are primarily ordering markers expressing precedence and succession, while “when” is more flexible and can encode simultaneity, a time frame, or a clause-level temporal relation. Ambiguity and context are central to interpretation, and tense and aspect can interact with the semantic reading, though the evidence here is stronger for the general claim than for a detailed grammatical interaction. The strongest supported claim is that these conjunctions are semantically tied to clause structure and discourse context, not just simple adverbials [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4][N3-R3].

The evidence clearly supports the subordinate-clause interpretation. The Scribbr entry explains that subordinating conjunctions introduce dependent clauses and that dependent clauses cannot stand alone as complete sentences [N1-R2]. The syntactic branch shows that “when,” “before,” and “after” are primarily subordinate-clause temporal markers, not standalone adverbs. They introduce or relate clauses in a sentence, often raising the complement to a higher position or treating it as a quantificational clause [N2-R1][N2-R4]. ### 3) Order of mention and discourse structure
Discourse and order-of-mention effects are central to how these conjunctions are interpreted. The discourse branch reports show that the order of events in discourse strongly affects perceived timing. People infer temporal order from underspecified information, and the sequence in which events are mentioned can create a mental model that shapes how simultaneity and succession are interpreted [N3-R3][N3-R2][N3-R4]. Simultaneous interpreting studies also show that interpreting processes analyze parallel source texts and interpretations and that temporal information is central to understanding the flow of events [N3-R2]. ### 4) Cross-linguistic and theoretical comparison
The cross-linguistic branch reports show that other languages mark simultaneity and sequence differently from English, and that the theoretical frameworks used to explain these patterns include temporal logic, discourse markers, and comparative linguistics. The evidence indicates that simultaneity and sequence are not encoded in a single universal way, but are realized differently across languages [N5-R1][N5-R4][N4-R1]. Theoretical frameworks such as temporal logic, discourse-marker theory, and temporal-reference studies explain these patterns. Discourse-marker studies show that temporal markers are often treated as triggers for discourse relations expressing temporal order [N5-R4]. Comparative linguistics and temporal-reference studies show that languages differ in how they mark temporal reference, including whether they use tense, aspect, or clause structure [N5-R1]. Together, these frameworks suggest that temporal expressions are best understood as a complex interplay of syntax, semantics, and discourse organization [N4-R1][N4-R5][N5-R4][N5-R1].

The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that cross-linguistic comparison is useful for identifying both universal constraints and language-specific strategies for expressing simultaneity and sequence [N5-R1][N5-R4][N4-R1][N4-R5].

### 5) Anaphora and referential integration
Anaphora and referential integration are crucial for interpreting these conjunctions. The anaphora branch reports show that temporal conjunctions connect to antecedent events or discourse referents. Temporal discourse markers such as “after,” “before,” or “while” are commonly described as triggers for discourse relations expressing a temporal relation, and the clause provides the clue to return to a previously mentioned thread in the discourse [N5-R4]. The German temporal discourse markers paper similarly argues that the after-clause serves a crucial function regarding discourse organization and that the temporal information conveyed by the clause provides the clue to return to a previously mentioned thread [N5-F4]. This shows that anaphora is essential for maintaining coherence and for anchoring temporal markers to the discourse.

The reports also suggest that “when,” “before,” and “after” differ in referential closure. “When” appears to be more referentially open because it can sometimes refer to a time frame, a point in time, or a clause-level relation, making it less immediately anchored to a single antecedent event [N2-R1][N2-R3]. In contrast, “before” and “after” are more directly tied to ordering two events, which can make them more closure-friendly in discourse because they specify a clearer relation to a preceding or following event [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The German temporal discourse markers study also shows that the after-clause can be topic- or background-related, indicating that referential closure depends on discourse position rather than a fixed syntactic role [N5-F4].

Anaphora can both resolve and create ambiguity. The discourse markers study notes that temporal markers are triggers for discourse relations, but the same marker may require a connection to the preceding context via a rhetorical relation such as background [N5-R4]. The German temporal discourse markers paper similarly states that the after-clause may require a connection to the preceding context via a rhetorical relation, and that the clause can be topic- or background-related depending on its position in the discourse [N5-F4]. The inferred-temporal-order study also shows that people infer temporal order from underspecified information, which means that anaphora and discourse context are essential for disambiguation [N3-R3]. The anaphora and discourse structure paper further argues that many adverbial phrases signal discourse relations between syntactically connected units, reinforcing that anaphora is a key mechanism for referential integration [N6-R1][N6-R2].

### 6) Integrated conclusion
Taken together, the branch reports support a unified conclusion: “when,” “before,” and “after” interact with syntax, semantics, and order of mention in a coordinated way. Syntactically, they are subordinate-clause temporal markers that introduce or relate clauses, often raising the complement to a higher position and interacting with tense and clause order [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R4]. Semantically, they encode precedence, succession, and in the case of “when,” sometimes simultaneity or a time frame; interpretation is sensitive to context, and tense and aspect can interact with the semantic reading [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4][N3-R3][N4-R3]. In discourse, order of mention affects perceived timing, prosody and anaphora help disambiguate sequence, and mention order can override or interact with explicit temporal markers [N3-R3][N3-R2][N3-R4][N5-R4][N5-F4]. Cross-linguistically, other languages mark simultaneity and sequence differently, and theoretical frameworks such as temporal logic, discourse markers, and comparative linguistics explain these patterns; cross-linguistic comparison helps distinguish universal tendencies from language-specific behavior [N5-R1][N5-R4][N4-R1][N4-R5]. Anaphora and referential integration are central to interpretation, with “when” being more referentially open and “before” and “after” more referentially anchored, while anaphora can resolve or create ambiguity [N5-R4][N5-F4][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2].

## Bottom line
These conjunctions are best understood as deeply integrated resources for expressing simultaneity and sequence. Syntax provides the clause structure; semantics provides the temporal relation; discourse and order of mention provide the context and coherence; anaphora provides the referential link; and cross-linguistic comparison shows that the patterns are neither universal in form nor purely language-specific in function [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4][N3-R3][N3-R2][N3-R4][N5-R4][N5-F4][N4-R1][N4-R5][N5-R1][N6-R1][N6-R2].
